articles.title: Structure and agency in emancipatory reform: A blueprint from a Black union
articles.abstract: The National Labor Convention of 1869, the first of its kind for African American workers, yielded a grand strategy for achieving full emancipation, in which those long subjected to domination might attain durable independence. Drawing upon decades of Black republican thought, this agenda combined macro‐level reforms targeting agrarian and industrial monopolies with micro‐level interventions into the habits of the working class. While the project fell short, its multivalent approach nevertheless offers republican theorists today a framework for better understanding the structural dynamics of domination and how to overcome them.

articles.title: On Liberalism’s Global Career: Dadabhai Naoroji and Representative Government
articles.abstract: This article reconsiders the relationship between the globalization of political liberalism and the globalization of political equality. Departing from interpretations of liberal theories of rights and representation as egalitarian or democratic, the article reconstructs an elitist paradigm of liberal representative government from the colonial world. It does so by offering a new reading of the thought of Indian political leader Dadabhai Naoroji. It recovers Naoroji’s overlooked commentary on political representation and imperial reform. I show that Naoroji drew upon analyses made by the first generation of Indian liberal thinkers about imperial political economy and mass-elite relations and used these arguments to formulate a distinctive model of electoral politics as a form of hierarchical tutelage. The recovery of Naoroji’s theory illustrates the deep tensions between representation and mass politics that marked liberalism’s global circulation.

articles.title: The Ambiguities of Ownership and Class: A Reply to Nicholas Vrousalis
articles.abstract: The article replies to Nicholas Vrousalis’s attempt to rescue radical republicanism from my critique that it fails on three counts: its non-contingency, domination, and structural injustice theses. Central to my response are the claims that (i) capitalist power cannot be reduced to legal ownership of the means of production, as the process of capitalization is constitutive of capital; (ii) neither neo-republican nor Kantian notions of domination adequately capture what is inherently wrong with capitalism, and (iii) the concept of “class domination” remains theoretically puzzling. I then defend an alienation-centered critique: capitalism’s mode of investment subjects citizens to an impersonal and anarchical form of governance, which, by being necessarily alienating, contradicts democratic self-determination. Overall, this critique forms the core of a “political, political theory of capitalism” and grounds the case for a specific kind of democratic socialism—socialism as reconciliation—which is more demanding than both republican and liberal socialisms.

articles.title: The Symbolic Politics of Housing
articles.authors: DAVID E. BROOCKMAN, CHRISTOPHER S. ELMENDORF, JOSHUA L. KALLA
articles.abstract: Voter opposition to development contributes to America’s housing shortage. Prevailing explanations emphasize NIMBYism (opposition to housing nearby) and homeowners’ self-interest. However, homeownership often fails to predict housing policy views, while NIMBYism offers little insight into support for policies that do not concern specific proposed housing projects—the focus of much recent policymaking. Drawing on symbolic politics theory, we argue that voters’ affect toward groups that housing policies make salient powerfully shapes their judgments about housing policies. We present evidence supporting this theory. Experiments show that affect toward developers and investors who build housing, government actors who approve it, and residents who move into it explain anti-development preferences when policies make these groups salient. Providing further causal evidence, short-form videos that manipulate affect toward developers have meaningful downstream effects on support for new development and permitting reforms. Ironically, voter dislike of the very actors who could ameliorate the housing shortage further exacerbates it.

articles.title: Polarization, crises, and accountability: The role of conditional partisan bias in economic perceptions
Caught in the crossfire: electoral spillover effects of accommodating the radical right
articles.authors: Jasmin Rath, Lukas Hetzer, Jan Berz, L. Constantin Wurthmann, Sarah Wagner
articles.abstract: Mainstream parties face mounting pressure from radical right challengers. While existing research highlights the electoral costs of accommodating the radical right, we know less about how this decision affects potential coalition partners. When mainstream parties accommodate, this generates spillover effects for potential coalition parties that may be perceived as complicit in legitimising the radical right. We test this mechanism in Germany, exploiting an Unexpected Event during Survey Design: the CDU/CSU’s announcement of tougher migration policy and signaled openness to AfD support. We examine how initial supporters of the CDU/CSU’s potential coalition partners changed their vote intentions in response. We find that the event increased switching from the SPD to The Left by approximately three percentage points, with a similarly directed but statistically insignificant effect for the Greens. These results demonstrate that accommodating the radical right affects not only the accommodating party itself, but the broader coalition landscape in multi-party democracies.

articles.title: Electoral reforms rejected: Partisan cues in an anti-party context
articles.authors: Todd Donovan, Caroline Tolbert, Olive Kuester
articles.abstract: Proposals to change how parties functioned in elections appeared on several American states’ ballots in 2024, often bundling nonpartisan primaries (NPPs) with ranked choice voting (RCV). Given the complexity of the proposals, voters faced a difficult task and may have relied on cues from campaigns when voting. We conducted a post-election survey to measure recalled exposure to campaigns and cues and model the role of cues in voting on these proposals. We find voters made choices consistent with partisan cues they report being exposed to. Democrats recalling Democratic elites were in favor were more supportive. Republicans who recalled a co-partisan elite being opposed were more likely to be opposed. We also used a survey experiment that manipulated exposure to partisan cues to test for effects of cues on support for NPPs and found results that corroborate what we observed with our self-reported survey data. Thus, even in an environment of mass anti-party sentiment, we find rules changes affecting parties may be difficult to pass via ballot measures when there is insufficient support among dominant party elites.

Do Appeals to the Diaspora Affect their Attachment to the Homeland? Findings from Jewish-Americans before and during the Israel-Hamas War
articles.authors: Yehonatan Abramson, Anil Menon, Alon Yakter
articles.abstract: Due to the growing importance of diasporas in contemporary geopolitics, many states seek to cultivate diasporic attachment and encourage diaspora mobilization using strategic narratives. Are such appeals effective? We report results from a pre-registered two-wave survey experiment conducted among Jewish Americans before and during the Israel-Hamas war. Our intervention assesses the impact of three common appeals identified by prior work: threats to the homeland, shared historical memory, and discrimination in the diaspora’s country of residence. We find that none of these appeals influenced Jewish-Americans’ attachment to, support for, or intent to mobilize for Israel, even during a war in the “homeland.” Instead, baseline differences in these outcomes reflect deep-seated generational, denominational, and partisan cleavages within the Jewish American community. These findings suggest that intra-diaspora fragmentation and long-standing views of the “homeland” might dominate short-term rhetorical interventions. Consequently, strategic frames deployed by kin states and political animators may be less effective on diaspora audiences than intended.

articles.title: The Labour Market Link: An explanation of Brexit support
articles.abstract: Where can we expect support for populist parties and initiatives to be weakest, and why? We argue support will be weakest in places that have experienced strong growth of employment in high-quality jobs, because such growth has positive spillover effects that shape wider perceptions of the economic status quo and the prevailing ideological climate. We test this proposition in relation to Brexit support at the time of the 2016 EU referendum and in the present day, using Census data to proxy the rate at which highly paid jobs replaced low- and mid-paid jobs in English and Welsh Local Authority Districts 1991–2016, and substantiate it at both the area and the individual-level. High-quality employment growth is a more powerful predictor of Brexit support than alternative local economic indicators and individual-level effects are sizeable. All else being equal, analysis of Understanding Society data shows the probability of Brexit support is only 30% among respondents in places that experienced very strong high-quality employment growth, compared to 55% among those in places with negative growth. These findings have important implications for how left behind places should be defined and for strategies that seek to address political discontent.

articles.title: Immigration and Nationalistic Attitudes: Panel Evidence from Chile
articles.abstract: Does rapid and large-scale migration fuel nationalism? Using administrative and panel survey data from Chile, we show that sudden, large-scale migration inflows increase identity-based nationalistic attitudes, such as national pride, among native-born citizens. These “immigration shocks” appear to activate perceptions of identity threat, leading to stronger expressions of national pride and belonging. Supplementary evidence from surveys, media reports, social media, and crime records suggests that this nationalism is predominantly exclusionary: areas most affected by migration also experienced spikes in anti-migrant rhetoric, hate crimes, and support for a newly formed far-right party. These findings underscore how rapid demographic changes can reshape political attitudes and contribute to the rise of exclusionary forms of national identity.

articles.title: Powers of ecological horror
Rejecting authoritarianism: When threats to democracy shape values
articles.authors: Amy Erica Smith, Mollie J. Cohen, Mason W. Moseley, Matthew L. Layton
articles.abstract: As politicians with authoritarian tendencies win elections globally, it becomes urgent to understand the social psychological mechanisms underlying support for such candidates. Prior research identifies authoritarianism as a likely predictor of vote choice. Contrary to views of authoritarian parenting as a stable, exogenous disposition, however, we argue that such attitudes can also evolve during campaigns, as voters take cues from elites. Analyzing AmericasBarometer data and a five‐wave panel study, this paper assesses authoritarian parenting values over Brazil's 2018 presidential campaign. Consistent with prior literature, authoritarian parenting attitudes early in the campaign predict who supported and opposed the authoritarian candidate Bolsonaro. However, these attitudes change over the campaign. This polarization is asymmetric, limited to Bolsonaro's opponents, who become increasingly anti‐authoritarian. The results illuminate how polities can resist authoritarian leaders and call for a reconsideration of authoritarianism in the public.

articles.title: Political psychology in an era of personalization: Misinformation research, generative AI, and the promise of tailored experiments
articles.abstract: Voters increasingly inhabit personalized information environments, where content, algorithms, and social cues vary across people. Yet popular approaches to studying and addressing features of information environments such as misinformation exposure often flatten this heterogeneity: Measures and interventions are developed for populations rather than individuals. Using misinformation as an illustrative case, I argue that population‐based methods for measuring and intervening on beliefs can obscure why some beliefs matter politically while others do not. I advocate for tailored approaches that adapt research designs to groups and individuals. Tailoring can increase relevance, facilitate persuasion, and create fruitful conditions for testing influential theories of opinion formation and change. I conclude by discussing the promise of a personalized political psychology that aligns measures and interventions with the idiosyncratic ways voters form and express opinions.

articles.title: Between reconciliation and peace making and brutalization: The Israeli case
articles.abstract: This article examines the relationship between peacemaking, reconciliation, and brutalization in violent conflicts. It argues that these processes are deeply interconnected: effective peacemaking and reconciliation can interrupt or reverse brutalization, whereas unsuccessful or incomplete peacemaking may allow brutalization to persist, deepen, and become normalized, even alongside formal reconciliation initiatives. This article is organized into two parts. The first one reviews the scholarly literature on peacemaking, reconciliation, and brutalization. It examines each process separately. Then proposes an analytical model that explains the emergence, escalation, and persistence of brutalization. Finally, it conceptualizes its relationship with peacemaking and reconciliation. The second part applies this model to the Israeli–Palestinian conflict, focusing on Israeli Jewish society in its confrontation with Palestinians in the Gaza Strip. This case study serves to illustrate the model and assess its explanatory value. Beyond examining peacemaking and reconciliation, the article's primary objective is to develop a comprehensive conceptualization of brutalization by defining its nature, identifying its underlying psychological and social mechanisms, and analyzing its antecedents and consequences for collective cognition, emotions, behavior, and norms.

articles.title: A blind spot for dominance? Why liberals underestimate dominant leaders more than conservatives
articles.abstract: The success of dominance‐oriented leaders often evokes surprise and dismay. We offer a psychological explanation beyond partisan reasoning, positing a systematic tendency among liberals to underestimate the appeal and efficacy of such leaders compared with conservatives. Drawing on moral foundations theory, we propose that liberals' heightened emphasis on harm avoidance and fairness explains their reduced liking for dominance‐oriented leaders, and that this reduced likability helps explain why they underestimate these leaders' prospects of success more than conservatives do. We test our predictions across multiple studies, including both political and organizational contexts, demonstrating that political liberals consistently perceive dominance‐oriented leaders as less likely to succeed than conservatives do—even when the leader's political affiliation is irrelevant, unknown, or aligned with their own. We conclude our investigation by suggesting that these diminished expectations from liberals might paradoxically enhance the success trajectories of dominant leaders.

articles.title: Climate change and conflict: The vicious cycles undermining climate action, and what can be done to break them
articles.authors: Boryana Todorova, Matthew J. Hornsey, Winnifred R. Louis, Kelly S. Fielding
articles.abstract: In this review, we synthesize evidence to argue that climate change and conflict are mutually reinforcing. We first examine conflict as a barrier to mitigation, focusing on four faultlines that slow climate action: (a) ideological polarization, (b) “elite versus ordinary people” narratives, (c) intranational, place‐based conflicts, and (d) international disputes. The consequence of these conflicts is worsening climate change, which in turn increases the prevalence of factors known to be conflict amplifiers: heat stress, economic stress, widening inequality, and forced displacement. Our analysis points to the potential for recursive “climate–conflict loops”, fuelled in part by erosion of institutional trust, shrinking moral circles, political polarization, and de‐prioritization of long‐term climate goals. In a spirit of optimism, however, we identify three buffers capable of breaking these vicious cycles: maintenance of procedural and distributive justice, enhancing information integrity, and scaffolding institutional cooperation. We conclude by proposing a research agenda that integrates psychological mechanisms into dynamic, multi‐level accounts of how climate impacts and political conflict coevolve.

articles.title: Solidarity between U.S. people of color: Synthesizing evidence, highlighting challenges, and proposing actionable solutions
articles.abstract: Mounting research establishes that solidarity between U.S. people of color (PoC) is triggered when a racially stigmatized ingroup believes they are discriminated similarly to another outgroup based on their alleged inferiority or foreignness . This heightened solidarity then produces political opinions and behaviors that benefit stigmatized outgroups who are not one's own—for example, Black adults become more pro‐Latino, Asian adults become more pro‐Black, and Latino adults become more pro‐Asian. This essay organizes, discusses, and synthesizes the overflowing evidence on this solidarity mechanism, paying special attention to its generality across stigmatized groups and political settings. The essay then highlights major pending challenges and opportunities to learn more about U.S. inter‐minority solidarity, emphasizing rival explanations, complementary pathways, and methodological pluralism. In parallel, this latter discussion illustrates the advantages of creating greater conceptual and theoretical synergy with comparativist research on ethnic identities and political conflict in nations across sub‐Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Western Europe. Finally, the article outlines new research agendas to deepen our understanding about U.S. inter‐minority politics, paying special attention to intra‐ group processes that regulate solidarity's vitality in an uncertain, complex, and threatening polity.

articles.title: A secondary bond: Why economic threats boost compensatory preference for government control in China
articles.authors: Ronghua Xu, Yi Ding, Yongyu Guo, Jan‐Willem van Prooijen
articles.abstract: Compensatory control theory suggests that threats to personal control increase the desire for external control. Yet, despite the growing salience of global economic instability—amplified by trade conflicts, protectionist policies, and heightened geopolitical tensions—empirical research has rarely examined this dynamic in the context of economic threats. Moreover, the direct psychological consequences of endorsing external control—whether it ultimately enhances or diminishes personal control—remain largely unexplored. Addressing both gaps, the present research focuses on the socio‐political context of China to investigate whether individuals facing economic threats and diminished personal control show increased preference for government control, a particularly powerful and salient external source of control in Chinese society. Across studies, the results showed a positive relationship between perceived economic threats and preference for government control, mediated by a reduction in personal control (Studies 1–3). Furthermore, we found that endorsement of government control helped enhance, rather than undermine, personal control (Studies 4 and 5). These findings suggest that government control serves as a compensatory source of control in response to economic threats.

articles.title: Private-sector support for programmatic candidates: evidence from a Senegalese election
articles.authors: Abhit Bhandari, Lucas Borba, Jessica Gottlieb
articles.abstract: Demand for clientelism in low-income countries distorts political incentives and constrains growth. Informal workers are seen as a strong clientelist constituency because they rely on forbearance and targeted benefits, yet they also constitute an electoral bloc that could coordinate in support of beneficial programmatic policies. We examine whether—and how—such demand for clientelism can be attenuated. We implement an information experiment with firm owners ahead of Senegal’s 2022 local elections, during which an upstart political faction campaigned on programmatic reform. Reminding informal workers of their coordination capacity reduced engagement with dominant clientelistic networks. This shift did not translate into support for programmatic alternatives but into political disengagement. Demand for clientelism can be mitigated, but programmatic mobilization remains a challenge.

The Role of Identity-Related Issues in Partisan Shifts Among White Americans, 2016–2020
articles.abstract: During the 2020 US presidential election, identity-related issues—immigration, racial justice, and white identity—were central to public discourse. This study examines how these issues shaped shifts in partisanship among white Americans who changed their affiliation from 2016 to 2020. Using American National Election Study panel data, we analyze how attitudes toward immigration, the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement, and white identity relate to Democratic Party, Republican Party, and Independent affiliations. We find that stronger white identity and restrictive immigration views increased the likelihood of switching to the Republican Party, whereas support for BLM increased the likelihood of identifying as a Democrat. These findings suggest identity-related issues played a key role in reshaping partisan alignments, especially in strengthening the Republican Party’s identity-based appeal.
